newsitem.title: BULGARIA: CORRUPTION MAY FAIL BULGARIA CURRENCY BOARD - NSS.
newsitem.headline: CORRUPTION MAY FAIL BULGARIA CURRENCY BOARD - NSS.

text.p: Bulgaria's National Security Service (NSS) warned on Tuesday against attempts by local business conglomerates to fail a restrictive monetary regime aimed at stabilising the collapsing economy.
"Opponents of the currency board are some big Bulgarian private business groupings connected to Bulgarian capital syphoned abroad," NSS director in charge Vladimir Manolov told a news conference.

Introducing an IMF-prescribed currency board system in July, which is a fixed exchange rate regime designed to stabilise the country's shaky banks and volatile currency is the new reformist government's first task.

The system bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks. The national currency, the lev, is pegged to an anchor currency at fixed rate and the amount of levs in circulation must be matched precisely by the foreign exchange reserves.
Failure to implement the system would result in Bulgaria not meeting international lenders' reform targets and ensuing suspension of agreed funding programmes.

"The conglomerates oppose all attributes of the currency board, which are: banned access to state money, strengthened control of bank transactions, impediments to investment of capital with dubious origin, transparancy of privatisation deals," said Manolov.
Capable of acting against the currency board are bank and company managers representing the emerging Bulgarian capital which has not yet consolidated its positions in the local economy, said Manolov.
A handful of powerful firms have sprung up in Bulgaria amid the legal and administrative chaos that followed the collapse of communism in 1989, which sometimes attracted negative publicity.

Politicians and economists attribute Bulgaria's current economic crisis to asset stripping of profitable state companies and syphoning of funds abroad by businesmen from the former Communist Party in the past seven years.
"Some of them promulgate their interests through local banks," said Manolov.

The NSS has started an investigation of the State Savings Bank on Tuesday, the country's biggest savings institution, after receiving signals that SSB funds were illegally transfered to a private commercial bank, said Manolov.

The service has estabilished a liquidity crisis in another currently operating bank and found irregularities in eight of 28 inspected financial brokerage houses, said Manolov. He declined to give further details.
"Results of our investigations are regularly given to the government," said Manolov.
In the past one year Bulgaria's central bank has placed in receivership and sought bankruptcies for 16 or one third of the country's banks after estabilishing their insolvency.
